pos: n. / adj. (a harsh cry; in the AV, the screech owl that shall rest in the ruins of Edom)
etymology: Imitative, from Middle English scrichen. At Isaiah 34:14 screech owl renders Hebrew lilith, a night creature — a bird of the waste places that finds a rest where a nation stood.
biblical_def:
Isaiah 34 is the burden against Edom, and its judgment is described entirely by who moves in afterward: The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest. The verses around it fill out the inventory — thorns in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses, an habitation of dragons and a court for owls, the cormorant and the bittern in possession, the line of confusion and the stones of emptiness stretched over the whole.

The phrase that carries the horror is the quietest one: the night bird shall find for herself a place of rest. Where a kingdom was, something now roosts comfortably. Scripture uses this picture more than once — Isaiah 13 does the same to Babylon, and Job in his misery says I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls, meaning that he now keeps the company of the ruins. The theological point is not ornithological. The desolate places in the prophets are always the consequence of a specific judgment on a specific pride, and the creatures are there to show that the judgment was total: not a city with fewer people, but a city with none, and a bird asleep in the palace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a harsh, shrill cry; the cry of an owl in the night.
webster_full: SCREECH, v.i. To cry out with a sharp shrill voice; to utter a sudden, sharp outcry, as in terror.
SCREECH-OWL, n. An owl whose scream is considered a bad omen; a bird of the night.
DESOLATE, a. Destitute of inhabitants; deserted; uninhabited; laid waste; in a ruinous condition.
BITTERN, n. A fowl of the grallic order, frequenting fens and marshes, noted for a booming cry.
CORMORANT, n. A large water fowl of the pelican kind, remarkable for its voracity.
scriptures: Isaiah 34:14
The wild beasts of the desert shall also meet with the wild beasts of the island, and the satyr shall cry to his fellow; the screech owl also shall rest there, and find for herself a place of rest.
Isaiah 34:13
And thorns shall come up in her palaces, nettles and brambles in the fortresses thereof: and it shall be an habitation of dragons, and a court for owls.
Isaiah 34:11
But the cormorant and the bittern shall possess it; the owl also and the raven shall dwell in it: and he shall stretch out upon it the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness.
Isaiah 13:21
But wild beasts of the desert shall lie there; and their houses shall be full of doleful creatures; and owls shall dwell there, and satyrs shall dance there.
corruption_summary: The prophetic ruin-scenes are treated as poetry with no historical reference, when the cities named were real, the judgments fell, and the sites can still be walked.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 34 and Isaiah 13 name specific nations — Edom, Babylon — and predict specific ends. The habit of reading these chapters as generalized poetic imagery about divine displeasure empties them of exactly what the prophets meant them to carry: a testable claim. Edom is gone. Babylon is a ruin field. The Reformed handling of prophecy has always insisted that the prophets spoke to real history and that history answered, which is why the confessions treat fulfilled prophecy as an evidence of Scripture's divine authorship rather than as a literary feature.

The other temptation is to turn the beast-lists into a bestiary and argue about whether lilith is an owl, a night-hag or a demon. The Hebrew is genuinely obscure and the AV made a reasonable choice; nothing in the doctrine hangs on the species. What the passage means is unmistakable whichever creature it is: the palaces have thorns in them, the fortresses have brambles, and a night bird has found a comfortable roost where a nation used to be. That is what the end of a proud people looks like from the outside, and the prophets describe it so that other proud peoples might hear it.
roots_summary: Hebrew lilith (H3917), a night creature; tsiyyim (H6728), desert beasts; shamamah (H8077), desolation.
roots_lines: Hebrew lilith (H3917) — a creature of the night; rendered screech owl, used once in Scripture.
Hebrew tsiyyim (H6728) — dwellers in the dry places; the wild beasts of the desert.
Hebrew qav tohu (H6957, H8414) — the line of confusion; the surveyor's cord of emptiness stretched over Edom.
Hebrew shamamah (H8077) — desolation, waste; the standing prophetic term for a judged land.
Hebrew tannim (H8577) — dragons or jackals; the habitation of the ruined palaces.
usage: “the screech owl also shall rest there” — something roosting where a kingdom stood.
“thorns shall come up in her palaces” — the inventory of a total judgment.
“the line of confusion, and the stones of emptiness” — a surveyor's cord over nothing.

pos: n. (the blowing of warhorses; the sound of the invasion heard from Dan)
etymology: Imitative, from Middle English snorten. At Jeremiah 8:16 it renders Hebrew nachrah, a snorting, from a root meaning to blow through the nostrils — used once in Scripture.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah reports the invasion first as a noise: The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein. Dan was the northern limit of the land, the top of the phrase from Dan to Beersheba, so the sound is at the border and has not yet arrived. The whole land trembles at a noise. Anyone who has heard cavalry at close quarters will recognize the detail: the snort of a warhorse before the charge is a sound designed by nature to unnerve.

Job, in the LORD's speech out of the whirlwind, gives the same animal a whole paragraph and one unforgettable line: Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils is terrible. The horse in Scripture is almost always a military animal, and the Bible's attitude toward it is consistent and unfashionable: the horse is magnificent, and trusting it is folly. Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. Jeremiah's snorting is the sound of a power Judah could not answer, and the chapter's own explanation of why it is coming has nothing to do with cavalry: they had healed the hurt of the daughter of the people slightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there was no peace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the forcing of air with violence through the nose, as a horse; the sound so made.
webster_full: SNORTING, n. The act of forcing the air violently through the nose; the sound made by a horse.
SNORT, v.i. To force the air with violence through the nose, so as to make a noise, as high spirited horses.
NEIGH, v.i. To utter the voice of a horse, called whinnying.
CAVALRY, n. A body of military troops on horses; a division of an army serving on horseback.
TREMBLE, v.i. To shake involuntarily, as with fear, cold or weakness; to quake; to quiver.
scriptures: Jeremiah 8:16

The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan: the whole land trembled at the sound of the neighing of his strong ones; for they are come, and have devoured the land, and all that is in it; the city, and those that dwell therein.
Jeremiah 8:17
For, behold, I will send serpents, cockatrices, among you, which will not be charmed, and they shall bite you, saith the LORD.
Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils is terrible.
Psalm 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
corruption_summary: Military and technological strength is trusted as though it were the decisive factor, which is exactly the confidence Scripture names as folly while never denying that the horses are terrible.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible is not naive about force. Job's warhorse paragraph is one of the great pieces of writing on the animal in any language, and Jeremiah reports that a whole nation trembled at a noise from the border. What Scripture denies is that force is where safety comes from. An horse is a vain thing for safety: neither shall he deliver any by his great strength. Israel's kings were forbidden to multiply horses to themselves, and Solomon broke the rule first and largest. The prohibition was not a dislike of cavalry; it was a fence against the confidence cavalry produces.

Jeremiah 8 makes the real cause of the disaster explicit, and it is not a shortfall in defence. The chapter is full of the failure of the men who should have spoken: they have healed the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there was no peace. A nation is not destroyed because the enemy's horses are loud. It is destroyed because the watchmen said everything was fine. The application is closer to home than the cavalry: where preaching has gone soft, the snorting at the border is already a mercy, because it is the last warning anyone is going to get.
roots_summary: Hebrew nachrah (H5170), a snorting; abbir (H47), a strong one, a stallion; sus (H5483), a horse.
roots_lines: Hebrew nachrah (H5170) — a snorting; used once, of the horses heard from Dan.
Hebrew abbir (H47) — mighty, strong; here the stallions whose neighing shook the land.
Hebrew sus (H5483) — a horse; almost always a war animal in Scripture.
Hebrew tsiphoni (H6848) — a cockatrice or adder; the serpents of the next verse, which will not be charmed.
Hebrew ra'ash (H7493) — to quake; the trembling of the whole land at a sound.
usage: “The snorting of his horses was heard from Dan” — the invasion arrives first as a noise.
“the glory of his nostrils is terrible” — the LORD's own description of the animal.
“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” — and where the trembling ought to stop.

pos: v. (to bite persistently; in Zephaniah, the judges are evening wolves that leave nothing till morning)
etymology: From Old English gnagan, to bite. At Zephaniah 3:3 it renders Hebrew garam, to break bones — a verb formed from the noun for bone.
biblical_def:
Zephaniah's indictment of Jerusalem does not begin with the people: Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves; they gnaw not the bones till the morrow. The last clause is the sharpest. An evening wolf, hunting at dusk, finishes the carcass in the night; there is nothing left to gnaw in the morning because nothing was left at all. That is the picture of a judiciary: not merely corrupt but thorough, taking everything, leaving no remainder for the next day's claimant.

Ezekiel uses the same animal for the same office — her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain — and Micah completes the picture of a whole leadership class on the take: The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD. That last clause is the worst of it, and it is the reason the prophets were sent. A corrupt bench that knew itself corrupt would be bad; a corrupt bench that leans upon the LORD and says none evil can come upon us is what brings the Babylonians. Zephaniah sets the standing contrast in the next breath: The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to bite by little and little; to bite off by degrees; to wear away by biting.
webster_full: GNAW, v.t. To bite by little and little; to bite off by degrees; to bite in agony or rage.
RAVENING, ppr. Devouring with rapacity; voracious; seizing the prey with violence.
WOLF, n. An animal of the canine kind, fierce, rapacious and destructive.
JUDGE, n. A civil officer invested with authority to hear and determine causes; one who declares the law.
BRIBE, n. A price, reward, gift or favor bestowed or promised with a view to pervert the judgment.
scriptures: Zephaniah 3:3
Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves; they gnaw not the bones till the morrow.
Ezekiel 22:27
Her princes in the midst thereof are like wolves ravening the prey, to shed blood, and to destroy souls, to get dishonest gain.
Micah 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
Zephaniah 3:5
The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame.
corruption_summary: Corruption in leadership is treated as a political problem rather than a covenant one, and the prophets' specific charge — men on the take who still claim the LORD is among them — goes unpreached.
corruption_paragraphs: The prophets aimed their hardest words at judges, priests and prophets — the three offices that were supposed to hold the nation to God's law — and the charge was always concrete: judging for reward, teaching for hire, divining for money. It was not vague institutional critique but the naming of a bribe. Micah then adds the thing that makes it unbearable: yet will they lean upon the LORD. They took the money and kept the theology, and the theology told them nothing bad could happen. That combination, not the bribery alone, is what Micah says will plough Zion as a field.

The application inside the church is direct, because the New Testament transfers the same standards to elders: not greedy of filthy lucre, not for filthy lucre's sake but of a ready mind. Peter and Paul both name money in the qualifications because they both expected it to be the pressure point. And the counterweight in Zephaniah is what any faithful officer should want written over his desk: The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not. Every morning. The wolves leave nothing by dawn; He brings out a fresh verdict at the same hour.
roots_summary: Hebrew garam (H1633), to break or gnaw bones; zeev (H2061), a wolf; ereb (H6153), evening.
roots_lines: Hebrew garam (H1633) — to break bones, to gnaw; formed from gerem, a bone.
Hebrew zeev (H2061) — a wolf; the prophets' standing figure for a predatory magistrate.
Hebrew ereb (H6153) — evening; wolves of the evening, hunting at dusk.
Hebrew betsa (H1215) — dishonest gain; Ezekiel's word for what the princes were after.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; what the LORD brings to light every morning.
usage: “her judges are evening wolves” — the office named by the animal.
“they gnaw not the bones till the morrow” — nothing left by morning.
“every morning doth he bring his judgment to light” — the contrast, at the same hour.

pos: n. pl. (wailing; what Amos says the songs of the temple shall become)
etymology: Imitative, from Middle English houlen. At Amos 8:3 it renders Hebrew yalal, to howl or wail — the sound of formal mourning, here replacing the sound of worship.
biblical_def:
Amos is shown a basket of summer fruit — ripe, and therefore at its end — and the word that follows turns the temple inside out: And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord GOD: there shall be many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast them forth with silence. The same building, the same voices, and a different sound coming out of them. Amos says the same thing again a few verses later in plainer terms: I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation.

Then comes the judgment that makes this chapter one of the most frightening in the prophets, and it is not an army: Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD. The final sentence on a people who would not hear is that they should not hear. They shall wander from sea to sea, and from the north even to the east, running to and fro to seek the word of the LORD, and shall not find it. Israel in Amos's day had prosperity, ivory houses, full feasts and loud music. What it was about to lose was the one thing it had never valued, and the howling in the temple is the sound of people discovering what silence costs.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): cries of distress; wailings; the loud protracted cry of grief or of a beast.
webster_full: HOWLING, n. The act of howling; a loud outcry or wailing; the cry of a wolf or dog.
HOWL, v.i. To cry as a dog or wolf; to utter a loud, protracted, mournful sound; to wail.
LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.
FAMINE, n. Scarcity of food; dearth; a general want of provisions sufficient for the inhabitants of a country.
SACKCLOTH, n. Cloth of which sacks are made; coarse cloth worn in mourning.
scriptures: Amos 8:3
And the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day, saith the Lord GOD: there shall be many dead bodies in every place; they shall cast them forth with silence.
Amos 8:10

And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation; and I will bring up sackcloth upon all loins, and baldness upon every head; and I will make it as the mourning of an only son, and the end thereof as a bitter day.
Amos 8:11
Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:
Zephaniah 3:5
The just LORD is in the midst thereof; he will not do iniquity: every morning doth he bring his judgment to light, he faileth not; but the unjust knoweth no shame.
corruption_summary: A famine of hearing the words of the LORD is not recognized as a judgment because it produces no visible hardship — the buildings stay full and the music stays loud.
corruption_paragraphs: Amos 8:11 describes a judgment that a prosperous religious culture is almost incapable of noticing. The famine is not of bread; nobody goes hungry. The temple still opens, the songs still go up, the feasts still run. What has gone is the word of the LORD, and by the time anyone looks for it, it cannot be found. Any age in which preaching has been replaced by something more immediately satisfying should read this chapter slowly, because the symptom of this famine is not distress but contentment — a full house that has not heard God speak in years and has not missed Him.

The prophets are consistent about what causes it. Amos 8 opens with men who cannot wait for the sabbath to be over so they can sell, who make the ephah small and the shekel great and falsify the balances, and who buy the poor for silver and the needy for a pair of shoes — and who kept the sabbath and the new moon punctiliously the whole time. Worship maintained alongside settled injustice is what God answers by taking His word away. The mercy in the passage is that it was preached at all: a people warned that the famine is coming has not yet begun it.
roots_summary: Hebrew yalal (H3213), to howl; shir (H7892), a song; raab (H7458), famine; hass (H2013), silence.
roots_lines: Hebrew yalal (H3213) — to howl, to wail; the sound the temple songs become.
Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song; the ordinary word for temple music.
Hebrew raab (H7458) — famine, hunger; sent here not for bread but for the words of the LORD.
Hebrew hass (H2013) — hush, silence; the bodies cast forth with silence.
Hebrew qayits (H7019) — summer fruit; the basket in the vision, and a pun on qets, the end.
usage: “the songs of the temple shall be howlings in that day” — the same voices, a different sound.
“a famine... of hearing the words of the LORD” — a judgment with no visible hardship.
“I will turn your feasts into mourning” — the calendar reversed.

pos: n. pl. (great creatures; in Lamentations 4:3, the sea monsters that nurse their young while Jerusalem's mothers do not)
etymology: From Latin monstrum, a portent or omen, from monere, to warn. At Lamentations 4:3 sea monsters renders Hebrew tannin, a great creature of the deep.
biblical_def:
Jeremiah is measuring the famine in the besieged city by comparing his own people with animals, and the comparison goes against them: Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. The great creatures of the deep nurse their young. The ostrich, in Job's description, leaves her eggs in the earth and is hardened against her young ones as though they were not hers. And Jerusalem, says the prophet, has become the second and not the first. The next verse spells out what he means: The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them.

The word in Hebrew is tannin, used across Scripture for great creatures — the ones God created on the fifth day and pronounced good, the serpent Aaron's rod became, the dragon of Isaiah's poetry, Leviathan in Job. The Bible has no category of independently evil beasts; every creature in it is God's, and the great ones are among the exhibits when He answers Job out of the whirlwind. Which is precisely what makes Lamentations 4:3 so terrible. The monsters behave as God made them to behave, and the covenant people, under the last extremity of a siege they were warned about for forty years, do not.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): unnatural productions; animals of huge or unusual size; in Scripture, great creatures of the sea.
webster_full: MONSTER, n. An animal of unnatural form, or of extraordinary size; anything out of the common course of nature.
WHALE, n. The general name of an order of animals inhabiting the ocean, the largest of created animals.
OSTRICH, n. A fowl of the largest size, of the African deserts, remarkable for neglecting her eggs.
SUCK, v.t. To draw with the mouth; to draw milk from the breast.
CRUEL, a. Disposed to give pain to others; inhuman; hard-hearted; void of pity.
scriptures: Lamentations 4:3
Even the sea monsters draw out the breast, they give suck to their young ones: the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness.
Lamentations 4:4
The tongue of the sucking child cleaveth to the roof of his mouth for thirst: the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them.
I am a brother to dragons, and a companion to owls.
Lamentations 2:11

Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city.
corruption_summary: The great creatures of Scripture are made into mythology or into demons, when the Bible files them among God's works and uses them as a standard by which His people are judged.
corruption_paragraphs: Two readings misplace the tannin. One treats Leviathan, the dragon and the sea monsters as borrowed Near Eastern myth, the residue of a chaos-combat story that Israel outgrew. The other makes them straightforwardly demonic, so that every mention becomes a spiritual-warfare text. Genesis 1 forecloses both: God created great whales, and God saw that it was good. They appear again in Job 41 as the LORD's own exhibit of a creature no man can draw out with a hook, and again in Psalm 104 as one He formed to play in the sea. They are creatures, magnificent and untamable, and they belong to Him.

That is what gives Lamentations 4:3 its edge. Jeremiah is not invoking a monster to horrify; he is citing a well-known fact about animals, that even the great creatures of the deep feed their young, and setting it against what the siege had made of his own city. Scripture repeatedly uses the ordinary faithfulness of creatures to shame the covenant people — the ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib, but Israel doth not know; the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times. The animals keep their instincts. Men break covenants, and the prophets make the comparison deliberately.
roots_summary: Hebrew tannin (H8577), a great creature, sea monster or dragon; ya'en (H3283), the ostrich; akzar (H393), cruel.
roots_lines: Hebrew tannin (H8577) — a sea monster, a great creature; created on the fifth day and called good.
Hebrew ya'en (H3283) — the ostrich; in Job hardened against her young as though they were not hers.
Hebrew akzar (H393) — cruel; what the daughter of the people had become.
Hebrew liwyathan (H3882) — Leviathan; the LORD's exhibit in Job 41.
Hebrew bath ammi (H1323, H5971) — the daughter of my people; Jeremiah's name for Jerusalem in the Lamentations.
usage: “Even the sea monsters draw out the breast” — an ordinary fact about animals, used to shame a city.
“the daughter of my people is become cruel” — the verdict of the comparison.
“the young children ask bread, and no man breaketh it unto them” — what it meant on the street.

pos: adj. (poisonous; of the viper that fastened on Paul's hand at Melita)
etymology: From Old French venimeus, from Latin venenum, poison. At Acts 28:4 it renders Greek therion, a wild beast, in a context the islanders clearly understood as deadly.
biblical_def:
Paul, shipwrecked and gathering sticks in the rain, is bitten: And when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand, they said among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live. The islanders read the event instantly and confidently, and they read it wrong. Their theology was simple — a man pursued by fate through a shipwreck and then a snake must be guilty of something — and it is the same theology Job's friends held with more sophistication. Then: he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm, and within the hour the same men changed their minds, and said that he was a god.

From murderer to deity in one paragraph, on the same evidence. Luke records it without comment, and the comment is not needed: this is what men do who read providence off the surface of events. Paul, for his part, does nothing with the incident at all — he shakes the snake into the fire and goes on gathering sticks, and the next thing recorded is that he prayed for the sick father of Publius and healed him. The sign in Mark 16 that believers shall take up serpents is fulfilled here in the only way the New Testament ever shows it: not sought, not staged, and not made into a doctrine, but survived on the way to something else.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): poisonous; noxious to animal life; having the quality of poison.
webster_full: VENOMOUS, a. Poisonous; noxious to animal life; as a venomous reptile.
VENOM, n. Poison; matter fatal or injurious to life; the poisonous fluid secreted by certain serpents.
VIPER, n. A serpent, a species of coluber, whose bite is venomous.
BARBARIAN, n. A man in his rude, savage state; among the Greeks and Romans, a foreigner, one not speaking their tongue.
VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense; retribution.
scriptures: Acts 28:4

And when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand, they said among themselves, No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he hath escaped the sea, yet vengeance suffereth not to live.
Acts 28:5
And he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm.
Acts 28:6

Howbeit they looked when he should have swollen, or fallen down dead suddenly: but after they had looked a great while, and saw no harm come to him, they changed their minds, and said that he was a god.
Mark 16:18
They shall take up serpents; and if they drink any deadly thing, it shall not hurt them; they shall lay hands on the sick, and they shall recover.
corruption_summary: Acts 28 has been made a proof text for handling snakes deliberately, when the passage shows an accident survived and Scripture forbids putting God to the test.
corruption_paragraphs: The snake-handling sects rest on Mark 16:18 read as an instruction, and Acts 28 read as a precedent. Both readings fail on the text. Mark's clause sits in a list of things that shall follow them that believe — signs that accompany, not exercises to perform — alongside drinking any deadly thing, which nobody proposes to attempt on purpose. And Paul did not pick up the viper; it fastened on him while he was doing chores. The governing word is our Lord's own answer to the devil on the temple pinnacle: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. A promise of preservation is not a permission to arrange the danger.

The more useful lesson is in the islanders. They drew a confident theological conclusion from a snake bite, and another, opposite conclusion from the absence of swelling, both within an hour, and both wrong. Reading God's favour or displeasure off the surface of events is the oldest mistake in the book — it is what Job's friends did, what the disciples did about the man born blind, and what the crowd did about the Galileans whose blood Pilate mingled with their sacrifices. Our Lord's answer in that last case is the standing correction: Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay.
roots_summary: Greek therion (G2342), a wild beast; echidna (G2191), a viper; dike (G1349), justice or vengeance personified.
roots_lines: Greek therion (G2342) — a wild or dangerous beast; the AV's venomous beast.
Greek echidna (G2191) — a viper; the creature named in verse 3.
Greek dike (G1349) — justice; the islanders' vengeance, a deity in their vocabulary.
Greek barbaros (G915) — a foreigner, one not speaking Greek; not an insult in Luke's usage.
Greek apotinasso (G660) — to shake off; what Paul did, into the fire.
usage: “when the barbarians saw the venomous beast hang on his hand” — and read it instantly, and wrongly.
“he shook off the beast into the fire, and felt no harm” — and went on gathering sticks.
“they changed their minds, and said that he was a god” — the same evidence, the opposite verdict.

pos: adj. (having long wings; of the great eagle in Ezekiel's riddle, which is Nebuchadnezzar)
etymology: English long + winged. At Ezekiel 17:3 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning long of pinion — part of an unusually detailed description of a bird that stands for an empire.
biblical_def:
Ezekiel is told to put forth a riddle and speak a parable, and it begins with a bird described in loving detail: Thus saith the Lord GOD; A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar. The reader is left to guess for nine verses, and then the interpretation is given plainly: Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon. The highest branch of the cedar is Jehoiachin; the second eagle is Egypt; and the vine that turns its roots toward the second eagle is Zedekiah, breaking the oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar by the LORD.

The chapter is a sustained lesson in how to read Scripture's figures: the symbolism is dense, the interpretation is supplied by the text itself, and the point is a moral one. God's charge against Zedekiah is not politics but perjury — seeing he despised the oath by breaking the covenant — an oath sworn to a pagan emperor and binding because it was sworn in God's name. And the chapter ends with the LORD announcing that He will do what the eagles did, but for good: He will take of the highest branch of the high cedar and plant it upon a high mountain, and it shall bring forth boughs and bear fruit, and under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): having long wings; in Scripture, of the great eagle of Ezekiel's parable.
webster_full: LONG-WINGED, a. Having long wings; as a long-winged fowl.
EAGLE, n. A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, remarkable for strength, size, flight and longevity.
PARABLE, n. A fable or allegorical relation of something real in life or nature, from which a moral is drawn.
RIDDLE, n. An enigma; something proposed for conjecture, or that is to be solved by conjecture.
CEDAR, n. A tree of the juniper or pine kind, of great size and durability.
scriptures: Ezekiel 17:3
And say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers, which had divers colours, came unto Lebanon, and took the highest branch of the cedar:
Ezekiel 17:12

Say now to the rebellious house, Know ye not what these things mean? tell them, Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof, and led them with him to Babylon;
Jeremiah 4:13
Behold, he shall come up as clouds, and his chariots shall be as a whirlwind: his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe unto us! for we are spoiled.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: Prophetic symbolism is treated as infinitely pliable, when Ezekiel 17 is the model of the opposite — a figure whose meaning the text itself fixes, and fixes to a single historical event.
corruption_paragraphs: A great deal of prophetic interpretation proceeds as though symbols were free-floating, to be matched against whatever the interpreter finds in the newspaper. Ezekiel 17 is a rebuke to the method. The eagle, the cedar, the branch, the vine and the second eagle all mean something exact, and the prophet is made to say what: the king of Babylon, the king of Judah, Egypt, and an oath that was broken. The Reformed rule of interpretation follows this pattern — Scripture interprets Scripture, the plainer passages govern the obscurer, and a figure means what its own context says it means.

The moral at the centre also deserves recovery. Zedekiah's crime, as God states it, was breaking an oath he had sworn to Nebuchadnezzar — a pagan king, an occupying power — and the LORD treats it as a sin against Himself because the oath was sworn in His name. That is a high doctrine of the binding force of a promise. A Christian's word, given to an unbeliever, in a matter that has become inconvenient, is under the same rule: he sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. And the chapter does not end in judgment. The last eagle is God, and what He plants on the high mountain bears fruit and shelters every wing.
roots_summary: Hebrew arek ha-eber (H750 / H83), long of pinion; nesher (H5404), an eagle or great vulture; chidah (H2420), a riddle.
roots_lines: Hebrew eber (H83) — a pinion, a wing feather; joined to arek, long, for longwinged.
Hebrew nesher (H5404) — the eagle or great vulture; the empire in Ezekiel's riddle.
Hebrew chidah (H2420) — a riddle, a dark saying; what the prophet was told to put forth.
Hebrew mashal (H4912) — a parable, a proverb; the second term of the commission.

usage: “A great eagle with great wings, longwinged, full of feathers” — a riddle with an exact answer.
“Behold, the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” — the answer supplied by the text.
“under it shall dwell all fowl of every wing” — the last planting, and it is God's.

pos: n. pl. (the hooves of warhorses; broken in Deborah's song by the prancings of their own mighty ones)
etymology: English horse + hoof, from Old English hof. At Judges 5:22 it renders a Hebrew phrase meaning the heels of the horse — the AV's only use of the compound.
biblical_def:
Deborah's song is the oldest poetry in the Bible and one of the most vivid, and this line is pure sound: Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones. Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron and Israel had none. The verse describes what became of them — hooves shattered by their own galloping, the strength that made the chariots terrible turned into the thing that broke them. The song says elsewhere how it happened: the river of Kishon swept them away, and the chariots of iron found themselves in mud.

The explanation Deborah gives is not tactical: They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera. Everything Israel lacked was supplied from a direction the enemy could not defend. The same pattern runs through the historical books — Gideon's three hundred, the hornet, the panic in the Philistine camp, the noise of chariots the Syrians heard when there were none. And the Psalm draws the standing lesson for the covenant people in a sentence they were meant to sing: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God. Judges 5 is that verse set to music with the wreckage still smoking.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the hoofs of horses; the horny substance that covers the feet of the animal.
webster_full: HOOF, n. The horny substance that covers or terminates the feet of certain animals, as horses and oxen.
PRANCE, v.i. To spring or bound, as a horse in high mettle; to ride with bounding movements.
CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a carriage with four wheels; a car used anciently in war.
MIGHTY, a. Having great bodily strength or physical power; very strong; valiant; bold.
BROKEN, pp. Parted by violence; rent asunder; shattered.
scriptures: Judges 5:22
Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings, the pransings of their mighty ones.
Judges 5:20
They fought from heaven; the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.
Psalm 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
Judges 5:24
Blessed above women shall Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite be, blessed shall she be above women in the tent.
corruption_summary: Judges 5 is treated as folk poetry rather than as the theological interpretation of a real battle, which is what a song in Scripture is for.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 4 gives the events and Judges 5 gives the meaning, and the pairing is deliberate. Scripture does this repeatedly — the Red Sea crossing and the Song of Moses, the deliverance and the psalm, the birth of Christ and the Magnificat. A song in the Bible is not decoration on a narrative; it is the inspired interpretation of it, telling the reader what the event meant and who did it. Treating Judges 5 as archaic folk material with no doctrinal weight loses the only place where the reader is told that the stars in their courses fought against Sisera.

The other thing the song is honest about is the cost and the ugliness. It blesses Jael for a tent peg, and it ends with Sisera's mother at the window counting the delay and being told by her wise ladies that the men must be dividing the spoil — to every man a damsel or two. Deborah puts that in. She lets the reader hear what the enemy expected to do to Israel's women, and lets that stand as part of the case. Scripture's war poetry does not pretend the wreckage is clean, and it never lets the credit for the victory rest with the winners.
roots_summary: Hebrew iqqebe sus (H6119 / H5483), the heels of the horse; daharah (H1726), a prancing or galloping; abbir (H47), a mighty one.
roots_lines: Hebrew aqeb (H6119) — a heel; joined to sus, horse, for horsehoofs.
Hebrew daharah (H1726) — a galloping, a prancing; used only here, twice in one line.
Hebrew abbir (H47) — mighty one, stallion; the war horses of Sisera.
Hebrew rekeb barzel (H7393, H1270) — chariots of iron; Israel's standing disadvantage in Judges.
Hebrew kokab (H3556) — a star; the ones that fought in their courses.
usage: “Then were the horsehoofs broken by the means of the pransings” — strength breaking itself.
“the stars in their courses fought against Sisera” — the explanation the song gives.
“Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” — the same doctrine, set to music.

pos: v. (hovers with beating wings; of the eagle over her young, and so of the LORD over Israel)
etymology: From Old English floterian, to float or flap. At Deuteronomy 32:11 it renders Hebrew rachaph, to brood or hover — the same verb used of the Spirit of God moving upon the face of the waters.
biblical_def:
The Song of Moses reaches for the one picture that will hold the whole wilderness history: As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings: So the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. Four verbs in order, and every one of them matters. She stirs up the nest — breaks up the comfort, makes the young leave. She flutters over them, hovering while they fall. She spreads her wings. She takes them and bears them. The disturbance and the catching are the same bird, and the whole of it is called leading.

The Hebrew verb behind fluttereth is rachaph, which occurs only three times in the Old Testament, and its most famous use is Genesis 1:2, where the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. The same brooding hover that was over the unformed creation is over the young eagles and over Israel in the desert. Moses had already used the image at Sinai — I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself — and Isaiah promises it forward to all who wait on the LORD: they shall mount up with wings as eagles. The point of the figure is the last clause of Deuteronomy 32:12: the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. No other bird was involved.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): moves the wings rapidly; hovers; flaps the wings without flying away.
webster_full: FLUTTER, v.i. To move or flap the wings rapidly, without flying, or with short flights; to hover.
HOVER, v.i. To hang over or about, fluttering with the wings; to hang about; to move to and fro near a place.
EAGLE, n. A rapacious fowl of the genus Falco, remarkable for strength, size, flight and longevity.
NEST, n. The place or bed formed or used by a bird for incubation or the mansion of her young.
BROOD, v.i. To sit on and cover, as a fowl on her eggs; to remain a long time in anxiety.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:11
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:
Deuteronomy 32:12
So the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him.
Exodus 19:4
Ye have seen what I did unto the Egyptians, and how I bare you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto myself.
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
corruption_summary: God's care is imagined as the absence of disturbance, when the eagle in Moses' figure begins by breaking up the nest.
corruption_paragraphs: The figure is usually quoted from the middle — borne up on eagles' wings — and the first verb is left out. As an eagle stirreth up her nest: she wrecks the comfortable place deliberately, because young that are never made to leave will never fly. Israel's wilderness was that stirring, and Moses is telling them so at the end of forty years. A believer who defines God's kindness as the absence of upheaval has taken one verb out of a sequence of five and will not recognize the hand that is actually leading him.

The hovering is the other half and must not be lost either. Rachaph, the verb behind fluttereth, is the brooding of the Spirit over the deep in Genesis 1 — a hovering that produces order out of what has no form. The same God who empties the nest is underneath the falling bird with His wings out. And the clause that closes the figure guards it from becoming sentimental: the LORD alone did lead him, and there was no strange god with him. Whatever the wilderness looked like at the time, there was never a second explanation for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew rachaph (H7363), to brood or hover; nesher (H5404), an eagle; ur (H5782), to stir up or rouse.
roots_lines: Hebrew rachaph (H7363) — to hover, to brood; used of the Spirit of God upon the face of the waters.
Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, to stir up; what the eagle does to her nest first.
Hebrew nesher (H5404) — the eagle; the figure Moses uses of the LORD in the wilderness.
Hebrew paras (H6566) — to spread out; of the wings under the falling young.
Hebrew nasa (H5375) — to lift, to bear; the last of the five verbs, and the one Israel remembered.
usage: “As an eagle stirreth up her nest” — the verb usually left out.
“fluttereth over her young” — the same word as the Spirit over the deep.
“the LORD alone did lead him” — no second explanation for the wilderness.

pos: n. pl. (low desert bushes; under one of which Hagar laid Ishmael down to die)
etymology: From Old English scrybb, brushwood. At Genesis 21:15 it renders Hebrew siach, a bush or shrub — the sparse scrub of the wilderness of Beersheba.
biblical_def:
The sentence is almost unbearably plain: And the water was spent in the bottle, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs. Hagar has been sent away with bread and a bottle of water; the water is gone; and there is one bush in the wilderness of Beersheba, and she puts her son under it for shade because there is nothing else she can do for him. The next verse is worse: she went and sat down over against him a good way off, about a bowshot, for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept.

What follows is the turn, and every word of it is deliberate: And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is. God heard the lad, not the mother, though the mother was the one recorded as weeping. And the remedy is the most ordinary thing imaginable: God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water. The well was already there. What she lacked was not water but sight, and the mercy was that God gave her the second so she could reach the first. Hagar had already named Him once, years before, at another well — Thou God seest me — and here He proves the name twice over: He sees, and He makes her see.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): low dwarf trees or woody plants; bushes; brushwood.
webster_full: SHRUB, n. A low dwarf tree; a woody plant less than a tree; a bush.
WILDERNESS, n. A desert; a tract of land or region uncultivated and uninhabited by human beings.
BOTTLE, n. A hollow vessel of glass, wood, leather or other material, for holding liquors.
BOWSHOT, n. The space which an arrow may pass when shot from a bow.
WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; a pit or cylindrical hole sunk into the earth to reach a supply of water.
scriptures: Genesis 21:15
And the water was spent in the bottle, and she cast the child under one of the shrubs.
Genesis 21:16

And she went, and sat her down over against him a good way off, as it were a bowshot: for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lift up her voice, and wept.
Genesis 21:17
And God heard the voice of the lad; and the angel of God called to Hagar out of heaven, and said unto her, What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is.
Genesis 21:19
And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water; and she went, and filled the bottle with water, and gave the lad drink.
corruption_summary: The Hagar narratives are read as evidence that the God of the Old Testament favours insiders, when the text shows Him twice going into the desert after a slave woman nobody else went after.
corruption_paragraphs: The charge is familiar: Abraham's household mistreats a foreign servant, and God endorses it. The text does not read that way. Hagar is the first person in Scripture to whom the angel of the LORD appears and the only person in Scripture who gives God a name — Thou God seest me. When she is cast out the second time, God hears the boy, calls her by name from heaven, asks her what ails her, tells her not to fear, opens her eyes, and promises to make of Ishmael a great nation. Sarah's conduct is recorded, not commended; and Abraham's grief is recorded too. What God does in the chapter is go into the desert after someone with no covenant claim on Him at all.

The narrative detail worth keeping is the well. It was there the whole time, a short walk from the shrub, and Hagar could not see it. God's answer to her extremity was not a new creation but opened eyes. A great deal of Christian experience runs along that line: the provision is nearer than the despair allows one to look, and the mercy asked for is sight. Elisha prayed the same prayer for his servant at Dothan — LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see — and the mountain had been full of horses and chariots of fire the whole morning.
roots_summary: Hebrew siach (H7880), a shrub or bush; chemeth (H2573), a skin bottle; beer (H875), a well.
roots_lines: Hebrew siach (H7880) — a bush, a shrub; the same word as the plants of the field in Genesis 2:5.
Hebrew chemeth (H2573) — a water skin; what was spent.
Hebrew beer (H875) — a well; what was there the whole time.
Hebrew shama (H8085) — to hear; God heard the voice of the lad — and gives Ishmael his name, God hears.
Hebrew paqach (H6491) — to open the eyes; the mercy Hagar actually received.
usage: “she cast the child under one of the shrubs” — the only shade in the wilderness.
“Let me not see the death of the child” — a bowshot away, weeping.
“God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water” — the well was already there.
